panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial contrast CT of a real patient (caption: 61-year-old female) showing a loculated lenticular left pleural empyema marked by the blue arrow, with pleural thickening/enhancement (split pleura sign) around the collection. This is the pleural component of empyema necessitans; the article title and caption attribute the process to thoracic empyema necessitans with per-continuitatem chest wall extension. B: Coronal contrast CT of the same real patient showing the left pleural empyema (white arrow) with expansion per continuitatem through the chest wall into the left chest and left upper abdominal quadrant (red arrow). Transpleural extension of a pleural empyema through the chest wall is the defining manifestation of thoracic empyema necessitans, matching the article title and caption; a specific manifestation is directly captioned for this panel.

in_text_mentions: workup included X-ray imaging of the chest and showed pleural effusion of the left side. Ultrasound of the swelling revealed a large abscess of the left chest with suspicion of communication to the pleural effusion. Following CT showed a pleural empyema with expansion per continuitatem to the left chest and left upper abdominal quadrant ( Fig. 3 ). Puncture of chest abscess formation revealed pus. Microbiological cultures returned positive for A. meyeri and Staphylococcus hominis . She was started on sulbactam and ampicillin and was urgently transferred to our hospital for further management.

The in-text description and image show an extensive abscess extending through the right chest wall (transpleural chest wall extension), right sixth rib involvement, and a loculated pleural collection, all specific manifestations of thoracic empyema necessitans. No panel letters are present, so the figure is treated as a single panel. [raw subtype: group_b_streptococcal_post_traumatic_pleural_fistula]

in_text_mentions: ng. Laboratory data showed a white cell count of 13,800/mm3, a C-reactive protein level of 296 mg/l, a serum glucose level of 462 mg/dl, and a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) concentration of 9.9%. Chest computed tomography (CT) scans on admission are shown in Fig. 1. These showed the fracture of the right sixth rib, a partially destroyed right middle lobe of the lung, and an extensive abscess through the right chest wall. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Frontal chest radiograph of a patient with empyema necessitatis showing a large left lower hemithorax pleural opacity (circled), consistent with a loculated pleural collection attributable to the target disease. B: Lateral chest radiograph from the same admission, showing the corresponding left-sided pleural opacity; supports the empyema necessitatis-related pleural collection.
